etymology: From Latin dis- (apart) + ad-grātum (pleasing-to) via Old French desagreer — "to be apart in mind."
biblical_def: To hold a different judgment than another. Not in itself sinful — Scripture records many faithful disagreements (Paul withstood Peter to the face, Paul and Barnabas parted over Mark, the Bereans examined the scriptures rather than swallowing whole what Paul preached). The biblical question is not whether disagreement occurs but whether it is conducted in love, truth, and right relation to the matter’s weight.
webster_summary: To differ in opinion or judgment; to be of unlike mind.
webster_full: To be at variance with another in judgment; to differ in opinion or sentiment. Not necessarily a breach of fellowship; brothers may disagree without dishonoring, and faithful disagreement is part of the iron-sharpening-iron of Christian community.
Distinguished from disregard: to disagree is to differ in mind; to disregard is to refuse attention or value. The two are often conflated; they are not the same.
scriptures: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
corruption_summary: Reframed as harm or disrespect; modern usage often equates disagreeing with the person with disregarding the person.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic age has reframed disagreement itself as harm. To say "I think you’re wrong about this" is increasingly heard as "I think you are unworthy." The collapse confuses two distinct biblical categories — disagreement (about judgment) and disregard (about dignity) — and the result is a culture where neither truth-telling nor mutual honor can survive.
Iron sharpens iron requires friction. The friction is not violation; it is formation. Recover the distinction and disagreement becomes a gift the body of Christ gives itself.
usage: To disagree is not to disrespect.
Iron sharpens iron — disagreement done well sharpens both.
Faithful brothers disagree on second-tier matters without breaking fellowship.

etymology: From dis- (away) + regard (to look upon, give weight to) — literally "to look away from, refuse weight to."
biblical_def: To refuse to attend to, value, or weigh another. A withholding of the dignity Scripture commands toward every image-bearer (Gen 1:27; James 2:8-9). Distinguished sharply from disagreement: disagreement differs in judgment; disregard withholds dignity altogether.
webster_summary: Not to regard; to slight; to neglect; to refuse weight to.
webster_full: To treat as unworthy of attention or consideration; to slight; to neglect; to refuse the dignity due. Active or passive: a man may disregard another by ignoring him, by dismissing him, or by treating his words and presence as if they did not require response.

Crucial distinction: you can disagree with someone fully while regarding them as fearfully and wonderfully made. The Christian discipline is to maintain regard precisely through disagreement — weighing the person even while differing from the position.
scriptures: But woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment and the love of God: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he.

If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well: But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
corruption_summary: Conflated with disagreement so that any contrary judgment is felt as withholding of dignity. Two distinct categories merged into one.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern conflation runs both ways. Some, eager to never be felt as disregarding, refuse to disagree at all — flattering, affirming, ducking the harder words. Others, eager to disagree freely, dismiss the felt-disregard of those they correct as oversensitivity. Both miss the pastoral discipline.

The biblical pattern is to disagree without disregarding. To weigh the person fully — their image-bearing dignity, their story, their burden — while still saying "I don’t think you’re right about this." Many feel disregarded when only disagreed with; pastoral patience is the slow work of teaching them the difference, while keeping the regard real and visible.

When someone says "you’re disregarding me," the loving response is rarely to back off the disagreement. It is to demonstrate the regard more concretely — eye contact, listening, time, prayer, presence — while holding the disagreement steady. Regard is shown in conduct; disagreement is held in conviction.
roots_lines: to look upon, take notice of
usage: To regard another is to weigh their full image-bearing dignity.
To disagree without disregard is the Christian discipline.
When someone feels disregarded, demonstrate regard concretely — do not abandon the disagreement to prove it.
